newsitem.title: USA: NHL ICE HOCKEY-FLYERS TO GO BACK TO HEXTALL IN GOAL FOR GAME 3.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY-FLYERS TO GO BACK TO HEXTALL IN GOAL FOR GAME 3.

text.p: The goaltender juggling continued for the Philadelphia Flyers Wednesday as coach Terry Murray tried to find a way to get his club back on track in the battle for the Stanley Cup before they run out of time.

The Flyers headed for Detroit Wednesday after losing the first two games of the best-of-seven NHL Stanley Cup finals at home -- first with Garth Snow in goal and then with veteran Ron Hextall between the pipes.
Following Snow's shaky outing in Tuesday's 4-2 defeat, Murray said Hextall, who spent most of the season as Snow's backup, would start Game 3 Thursday in Detroit.
"I'm going to put Hextall back in goal," Murray said.
After three playoff rounds in which Murray enjoyed solid goaltending from both of his netminders, the coach was unable to hide his current frustration.
"We have to get better in goal, have to make the big stops," Murray said.
"Hextall let in a long goal in Game 1, which took us out of the game, and Snow allowed an unscreened goal that he should have stopped in Game 2 that was the winner.

"But I'm going to go with the veteran," Murray said of Hextall, who won the last three games of the Eastern Conference finals against the New York Rangers and was in goal for the Flyers the last time they were in the finals in 1987.
"At times, Snow seemed tentative. Obviously, we have to play better in front of Hextall," added Murray, who was looking for any silver lining he could grasp.
"We have been good on the road all year, so maybe getting away will help."
The Red Wings have no such goaltender headaches with Mike Vernon playing at a level that makes him a strong Conn Smythe Award candidate, given to the most valuable player of the playoffs.

Vernon, who backstopped Calgary to the Stanley Cup in 1989, is 14-4 in the playoffs with a stellar 1.84 goals against average. His 14 victories is one more than he recorded in the regular season as backup to Chris Osgood.

"I rested most of the year, so even at 34 I'm real fresh and want to play every game now," said Vernon, who had the forethought to add a clause to his $2.3 million contract that assured it would be renewed if he wins the Stanley Cup.
Vernon credited some of his success to the superb defensive play of his teammates throughout the playoffs.
"I'm focused and there haven't been too many second shots," he said. "This seems easier than when we won in 1989 with the Calgary Flames."
Detroit coach Scotty Bowman said the reason the Wings have a 2-0 lead over Philadelphia: "Vernon has been better than their goalies."
"So far we really haven't played as good as in the previous series," Bowman said of Detroit's sensational play in upending the defending champion Colorado Avalanche.
Now these Red Wings have a chance to erase the memory of the 1942 and 1966 finals collapses when Detroit became the only team to win the first two games on the road only to lose the Stanley Cup.

"I was in the Montreal organisation at the time of the 1966 comeback," recalled Bowman. "Henri Richard turned that series around. It broke (Detroit defencema) Bill Gadsby's heart. He played 20 years, made the Hall of Fame, and never won a Stanley Cup ring. That was his last year."
But Bowman said this team was not thinking about the franchise's past failures as they try to bring the Stanley Cup to Detroit for the first time since 1955.
"We are not trying to banish those ghosts," Bowman said.
"We wanted to beat Colorado in the worst way because they had embarrassed a team which won (a record) 62 games last year, but that's the only ghosts we have.
"And we have already accomplished that."
